So, if you would like to be funded for 18 months of operations with an average of five engineers, then you will need about 15k x 5 x 18 = $1.35mm... Simply answer that you are raising for N months (usually 12-18) and will thus need $X, where X will usually be between $500k and $1.5 million." On dilution: "If you can manage to give up as little as 10% of your company in your seed round, that is wonderful, but most rounds will require up to 20% dilution and you should try to avoid more than 25%."
value: $15k/engineer/month all-in; 15k x 5 x 18 = $1.35mm; raise for N months (usually 12-18) needing $X, usually between $500k and $1.5 million; seed dilution: 10% wonderful, most rounds up to 20%, avoid more than 25%

statement: YC specifies the leave-behind package: "The executive summary should be one or two pages (one is better) and should include vision, product, team (location, contact info), traction, market size, and minimum financials (revenue, if any, and fundraising prior and current)."
value: 1-2 pages (1 preferred); 6 required elements

statement: Sequoia's business-plan/pitch guide — the template Airbnb used — lists exactly 10 sections in this order: Company purpose ("define your company in a single declarative sentence"), Problem, Solution, Why now?, Market potential, Competition / alternatives, Business model, Team, Financials, Vision ("If all goes well, what will you have built in five years?"). On financials the entire instruction is: "If you have any, please include."
value: 10 sections

statement: a16z states its preference and shows the arithmetic of why top-down fails: "we like seeing a bottoms-up analysis, which takes into account your target customer profile, their willingness to pay for your product or service, and how you will market and sell your product. By contrast, a top-down analysis calculates TAM based on market share and a total market size." The worked example: "If I can sell a $1 toothbrush every year to 40% of the people in China, my TAM is 1.36B people x $1/toothbrush x 40% = $540M/year. This analysis not only tends to overstate market size (why 40%?), it completely ignores the difficult (and expensive!) reality of getting your toothbrush into the hands of 540M toothbrush buyers."
value: 1.36B people x $1/toothbrush x 40% = $540M/year (verbatim as published by a16z; note a16z's own arithmetic is loose — 1.36B x 40% is 544M, so the strictly correct product is $544M)

statement: YC's Michael Seibel gives the same top-down/bottom-up distinction and states a preference with the specific failure mode: "With the top down approach you determine the total market and estimate your potential share of it. With bottom up you figure out where comparable products are sold, how many of them are sold, and what % of those sales you could take. I prefer the bottom up method because it helps you avoid a common top down pitfall, which is not narrowing down the customer enough... that could mean assuming all women are in your market - no matter their age or nationality."
value: 2 methods (top down and bottom up); bottom up preferred

statement: Seibel condenses the entire seed pitch to seven questions: (1) What do you do? (2) How big is the market? (3) What's your progress? (4) What's your unique insight? (5) What's your business model? (6) Who's on your team? (7) What do you want? On progress — the pre-traction answer — he writes: "What I'm trying to understand here is how fast you produce work. What is the ratio between what you've done and how long you've been working on it?... I also tend to value product development and customers first and other things such as fundraising or biz dev deals a distant second."
value: 7 questions

statement: DocSend's own research states: "We see VCs spend an average of three minutes and 20 seconds reviewing seed pitch decks," and recommends deck length: "We've found that building a 19-20 page deck with the following sections is the best way to catch the attention of busy investors." The article is titled "Sealing the deal in 12 slides" and prescribes 12 sections, noting "founders who open their decks with the first four sections above are more likely to raise funding than those who opt for other approaches" (company purpose, problem, solution, market size).
value: 3 min 20 sec; 19-20 pages; 12 sections

statement: DocSend publishes per-section dwell times for seed decks, which rank the slides investors actually stop on. Business model 64 seconds (the longest; "This section gets the longest look from VCs"); Product 59 seconds; Traction 40 seconds; Team 38 seconds; Financials 37 seconds; Problem 34 seconds; Solution 34 seconds; Competition 34 seconds; Fundraising ask 32 seconds; Market size 29 seconds; Company purpose 26 seconds; Why now? 23 seconds.
value: Business model 64s, Product 59s, Traction 40s, Team 38s, Financials 37s, Problem 34s, Solution 34s, Competition 34s, Fundraising ask 32s, Market size 29s, Company purpose 26s, Why now? 23s

statement: DocSend's strongest failure signal: "We found that VCs spend 80 percent more time evaluating the traction of companies that didn't raise money successfully. If your market traction isn't immediate to investors, it may raise skepticism and prompt more inspection that may not work out in your favor." On what counts as traction pre-launch: "You can include letters of intent, testimonials, customer pipeline, and beta feedback as appropriate to your product's stage."
value: 80% more time on traction of decks that failed

statement: DocSend's pre-seed research: "we found that 92% of successful decks globally — and 100% in the West Coast of the US — had a slide explaining the problem that the product or company set out to solve." Average section lengths in successful pre-seed decks: problem 1.8 slides, product 2.8 slides. "According to our research about 60% of companies include this [traction] section in their decks." Overall: "investors spend less than 3.5 minutes on average on each pre-seed pitch deck... the best way to do this is with a 20 page deck that follows a clear narrative outline."
value: 92% include a problem slide (100% West Coast); 1.8 problem slides; 2.8 product slides; ~60% include traction; 20 pages; <3.5 min — all verbatim from DocSend. Caveat: DocSend's own stat boxes on the same page say 1.9 problem pages, 2.7 product pages, and 59% traction.

statement: DocSend's Startup Index seed report tracks the canonical review-time number falling over time: "In 2019, the average amount of time VCs viewed decks was 3:27 vs. 3:44 in 2015. This time spent metric has steadily declined throughout 2020." Deck length did not move: "The number of slides in a pitch deck used to raise a successful Seed round remains unchanged at 20 slides." Process: successful founders in 2019 contacted 77 investors on average and held 40 meetings; unsuccessful founders contacted 70 and averaged 15 meetings.
value: 3:44 (2015) → 3:27 (2019); 20 slides; 77 contacts / 40 meetings (successful), 70 contacts / 15 meetings (unsuccessful)

statement: DocSend's weekly Pitch Deck Interest metric — the most recent published time-on-deck data — shows average review time settling well below the famous 3:44: it held at "2 minutes, 30 seconds" for most of Q1 2024, was "2 minutes, 24 seconds" at the start of Q2, and fell to "2 minutes, 18 seconds" in both April and June 2024, described as VCs who "raced through pitch decks."
value: 2 min 18 sec – 2 min 30 sec (2024). Explicit weekly values on DocSend's Pitch Deck Interest "Investor Time Spent" metric: 2:30 on Jan 9, Jan 16, Jan 29, Feb 26, Mar 4, Mar 11, Mar 18, Mar 25 and Jun 3, 2024; 2:24 on Apr 8, 2024 (start of Q2); 2:18 on Apr 15, 2024 and Jun 10, 2024. The Jun 10, 2024 reading of 2:18 is the last time-on-deck figure DocSend ever published.

statement: In "The Insider's Guide to Data Rooms: What to Know Before You Raise" (a16z, August 25, 2022), Justine Moore lists five things a16z often sees in data rooms but wouldn't recommend including "unless an investor specifically asks for them," under the heading "What shouldn't you include?" Two of them: "Detailed 3- to 5-year financial projections. This may be a controversial one, but it's often difficult to model forward-looking financials for early stage consumer companies. We love to hear the key milestones you're looking to hit in the coming 12-18 months (and what you'll need to get there), but we don't expect a fully-baked model." And: "Market sizing. We'll do our own work sizing the market. There are rare cases where you may want to include this (for example, if you're in an obscure market and it's hard to find publicly available data)."
value: Figure unchanged and exact: 0 years of financial projections required ("Detailed 3- to 5-year financial projections" is listed among things a16z would NOT recommend including), with "key milestones you're looking to hit in the coming 12-18 months" wanted instead. Market sizing is likewise on the do-not-include list. CORRECTION TO THE CITATION: the author is Justine Moore, not Olivia Moore; published August 25, 2022.

statement: a16z gives three concrete honesty rules for any numbers you do show. Anchoring: "In most cases, your projections shouldn't be vastly different from the historical data. If MAUs have grown ~20% MoM for the past six months, it's probably unrealistic to assume 200% MoM growth for the next year." Accountability: "make sure that you're fairly confident in your ability to achieve your projections. If an investor passes on your current round but wants to reconnect for later rounds, you want to be able to say that you beat or exceeded your plan." Labeling: "make sure it's clear where historicals end and future projections begin by highlighting projections in a different color, or adding an (A) after actuals and a (P) after projections." It also names the killer inconsistency: "your deck says $2M in ARR, but your model shows $1.5M."
value: 20% MoM historical vs 200% MoM projected — confirmed verbatim. (Byline correction: the author is Justine Moore, not Olivia Moore.)

statement: Paul Graham's essay in the YC library defines what a deck must establish and how fast: "You need three things: formidable founders, a promising market, and (usually) some evidence of success so far." On the window: "Most investors decide in the first few minutes whether you seem like a winner or a loser, and once their opinion is set it's hard to change." He defines TAM bottom-up: "If there are x number of customers who'd pay an average of $y per year for what you're making, then the total addressable market, or TAM, of your company is $xy. Investors don't expect you to collect all that money, but it's an upper bound on how big you can get." And sets the pre-launch bar: "A three month old company at Demo Day only needs to be a promising experiment that's worth funding to see how it turns out."
value: 3 things (formidable founders, a promising market, and usually some evidence of success so far); investors decide in the first few minutes; TAM = x customers × $y per year = $xy

statement: CRV, a seed-stage venture firm, published in June 2026: "Most successful early stage decks run around 10 to 15 slides for the core presentation. At seed, this typically covers problem, solution, traction, unique insight, business model, market size, team and the ask." On placement: "Successful decks often include a traction teaser on the first 2 or 3 slides to establish credibility immediately, then expand on the numbers later in the deck." On financials: "Detailed technical explanations, financial models and supporting data belong in the appendix or data room, not the core presentation." On the most common structural error: "Overloading slides with multiple points is a common structural error. Each slide should communicate one clear idea."
value: 10-15 core slides; traction teaser in first 2-3 slides

statement: MAG Interactive reported QuizDuel ARPDAU of 9.0 US cents for the nine months to May 2026 (+31% year on year), 8.8 cents in Q3, with DAU 0.9M (-12%) and MAU 2.2M (-9%); revenue is IAP plus ads.
